title: Default alive: how Gobble turned $1M/mo burn into profit by cutting marketing and trusting cohorts
summary: A conversation with Gobble founder Ooshma Garg, where Garry (a board member) frames what to do when a flailing competitor's IPO kills your fundraising: test whether you're already profitable. Covers proprietary IP for retention, cohort retention as the key health metric, and why founders should try profitability before selling or shutting down.

principles.text: Early on, startups are judged by popularity (voting machine); later, by what cash the business throws off (weighing machine).
principles.quote: The game is a, it's a popularity contest early. It's basically a voting machine early, and then later, it becomes a weighing machine.

principles.text: When you can't raise, try profitability before selling, shutting down, or recapping; it restores your leverage.
Cohort retention reveals the true health of a business; the best brands' curves flatten to an asymptote.
principles.quote: I think cohort retention is one of the most important tools for every founder because it really tells you the health of the business, period, as a brand, as a going concern.

principles.text: Digital ad channels have depth limits: the first customers are targeted and sticky, but marginal customers get worse, especially with heavy capital.
principles.quote: in the search for more and more marginal customers, you're actually getting customers that are worse.

principles.text: Founders have a growth knob: burn cash to grow faster, or grow slower and sustainably, even profitably.
principles.quote: There are lots of places where the founder has this growth knob, they can choose, do we grow faster and burn a lot more money or do we grow slower but much more sustainably?

principles.text: Always try going profitable; Garry regrets never charging at Posterous despite massive usage.
principles.quote: So always remember, you can go profitable, or at least you can try and it's a very important tool for the tool belt and we should have tried, we never did.
